Now that you are holding onto a Node you have a few responsibilities:

First, you must read from the Node.Ready() channel and process the updates
it contains. These steps may be performed in parallel, except as noted in step
2.

1. Write HardState, Entries, and Snapshot to persistent storage if they are
not empty. Note that when writing an Entry with Index i, any
previously-persisted entries with Index >= i must be discarded.

2. Send all Messages to the nodes named in the To field. It is important that
no messages be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk,
and all Entries written by any previous Ready batch (Messages may be sent while
entries from the same batch are being persisted). To reduce the I/O latency, an
optimization can be applied to make leader write to disk in parallel with its
followers (as explained at section 10.2.1 in Raft thesis). If any Message has type
MsgSnap, call Node.ReportSnapshot() after it has been sent (these messages may be
large).

Note: Marshalling messages is not thread-safe; it is important that you
make sure that no new entries are persisted while marshalling.
The easiest way to achieve this is to serialize the messages directly inside
your main raft loop.

3. Apply Snapshot (if any) and CommittedEntries to the state machine.
If any committed Entry has Type EntryConfChange, call Node.ApplyConfChange()
to apply it to the node. The configuration change may be cancelled at this point
by setting the NodeID field to zero before calling ApplyConfChange
(but ApplyConfChange must be called one way or the other, and the decision to cancel
must be based solely on the state machine and not external information such as
the observed health of the node).

4. Call Node.Advance() to signal readiness for the next batch of updates.
This may be done at any time after step 1, although all updates must be processed
in the order they were returned by Ready.

Second, all persisted log entries must be made available via an
implementation of the Storage interface. The provided MemoryStorage
type can be used for this (if you repopulate its state upon a
restart), or you can supply your own disk-backed implementation.

When Asynchronous Storage Writes is enabled, the responsibility of code using
the library is different from what was presented above. Users still read from
the Node.Ready() channel. However, they process the updates it contains in a
different manner. Users no longer consult the HardState, Entries, and Snapshot
fields (steps 1 and 3 above). They also no longer call Node.Advance() to
indicate that they have processed all entries in the Ready (step 4 above).
Instead, all local storage operations are also communicated through messages
present in the Ready.Message slice.

The local storage messages come in two flavors. The first flavor is log append
messages, which target a LocalAppendThread and carry Entries, HardState, and a
Snapshot. The second flavor is entry application messages, which target a
LocalApplyThread and carry CommittedEntries. Messages to the same target must be
reliably processed in order. Messages to different targets can be processed in
any order.

Each local storage message carries a slice of response messages that must
delivered after the corresponding storage write has been completed. These
responses may target the same node or may target other nodes.

items.rationale:
Reviewed fixed artifact e16a1086134847b5b883f40456d6f762 version 1, its plan, executable inputs, accepted claim/bindings version 1 and execution eff178129dba40e5bb813284a477729d. Applicability comes from raft.proto: implicit mode assigns automatic exit to Raft, whereas explicit mode assigns the exit proposal to the application. Generic proposal-loss permission does not turn this internal automatic transition into a caller-owned retry. The check observes configuration completion, not user-command completion or transfer success.

The driver uses actual three-node RawNode state machines from identical configured genesis snapshots. Campaign produces real votes, self-votes pass through persistence and Advance, and all configuration entries come from actual committed Ready work. MemoryStorage substitutes the application storage layer under a no-crash model; no protocol state, term, progress or acknowledgment is fabricated. Each Ready is persisted and its committed entries applied before Advance or message delivery. ApplyConfChange followed by TransferLeader before Advance is legal sequential access; Node.run independently demonstrates that messages can be processed during an outstanding Ready. The driver drops actual MsgTimeoutNow only. Exactly one such packet is reported lost; quorum messages are delivered. The fixed scenario therefore preserves the original overlap rather than delaying transfer until after automatic exit has already been scheduled.

Each case has one admission and one result with independent identity (case, joint_index=3); neither term nor the compared outgoing count is an equality identity filter. The monitor explicitly selects admission_alias=admission. Actual parser output has no parsing errors, correlates control result event 6 with admission 2 and transfer result 16 with admission 12, and evaluates both. The prerequisite establishes installed implicit joint state, not the final expected answer. Results are emitted after the fixed tick/drain loop regardless of outcome. No control failure or expected-state filter removes the violating observation.

The control produced one exit entry and applied index 4, with outgoing=0. The transfer history admitted the same joint entry at commit 3 while leadTransferee=2, then acknowledged application to 3. At tick 10 the transferee was zero. At tick 40 the same term-2 leader remained, heartbeat counts were 40 from each follower, all queued work was drained, applied=commit=last=3, outgoing=3, AutoLeave=true, and exit_entries=0. Thus the comparison is a completed bounded non-completion measurement, not a runner timeout or missing result. The later ordinary proposal occurs strictly after result and causes one exit entry and application through index 5; this is contrary evidence against permanent inability to reconfigure, and evidence that new application work supplies the trigger.

The numeric horizon is not itself a normative deadline. Correspondence to lost autonomous retry also rests on the sourced transition structure: appliedTo is the automatic-exit producer; Step rejects its proposal while transfer is pending; timeout calls abortLeaderTransfer, which only clears the transferee. With all existing log work applied, empty Ready/Advance does not create MsgStorageApplyResp. In the observed stable, caught-up cluster, periodic heartbeat/response and quorum-check branches do not append entries or call appliedTo. No snapshot or new authority arises in this schedule. Continuing this same serviced quiescent regime therefore provides no autonomous retry trigger; unrelated client work or a new election changes the regime. This source-supported explanation makes the finite witness relevant to the accepted automatic-retry responsibility without inventing a 40-tick service guarantee. The original cause hypothesis is supported for this history; broader availability or safety consequences are not measured. The control and rescue are explained alternatives, already addressed above, rather than unresolved conflicts with the scoped missing-trigger conclusion. The unspecified API deadline remains an explicit scope limitation, not a claimed timing guarantee.
